Opening prayer: Tulsidas cleans the mirror of his mind with his Guru's blessing before singing Ram's glory.
Knowing his own limits, he asks Hanuman for strength, wisdom and freedom from troubles.
Praise of Hanuman: Ram's messenger, son of Anjani and the Wind, a hero of matchless strength.
Hanuman's appearance: golden body, earrings, curly hair, thunderbolt and flag in hand.
Hanuman's nature: learned and clever, always eager to do Ram's work and to hear Ram's story.
Hanuman in the Ramayan: tiny before Sita, fearsome when burning Lanka, mighty against the demons.
Hanuman brings the Sanjivani herb to save Lakshman; Ram embraces him as dear as his brother Bharat.
Gods, sages and poets all fail to describe Hanuman's full glory.
Hanuman's help to others: he brings Sugriv to Ram, and Vibhishan becomes king of Lanka on his advice.
Hanuman's wonders: as a child he swallowed the sun; with Ram's ring in his mouth he crossed the ocean.
Hanuman guards Ram's door; every hard task becomes easy by his grace.
Whoever takes his refuge finds joy; ghosts, illness and pain flee at his name.
Hanuman serves Ram, the king of all, and fulfils every sincere wish of his devotees.
Sita blessed Hanuman to grant the eight powers and nine treasures; devotion to him leads to Ram.
Remembering Hanuman cuts away every trouble.
Closing: Tulsidas asks Hanuman to bless him like a Guru and to live in his heart.
Final prayer: may Hanuman dwell in the heart along with Ram, Lakshman and Sita.
Opening prayers to Ram and to Hanuman before the story of Sunderkand begins.
On the seashore, encouraged by Jambavan, Hanuman asks the monkeys to wait for him and sets off.
Hanuman climbs a mountain by the sea and leaps toward Lanka, swift as Ram's arrow.
The ocean sends Mount Mainak up to give Hanuman rest; he touches it but will not stop until Ram's work is done.
The gods send Surasa, mother of serpents, to test Hanuman's strength and wisdom. She wants to eat him.
Surasa opens her mouth wider and wider; Hanuman keeps doubling his size.
Then Hanuman becomes tiny, darts into her mouth and out again. Pleased, Surasa blesses him.
A demoness in the sea catches flying creatures by grabbing their shadows on the water.
She tries this on Hanuman; he sees through the trick, kills her and lands on Lanka's shore.
Hanuman admires the forest by the shore, then climbs a hill to look at Lanka.
He sees Lanka: a golden fortress surrounded by the sea, beautiful and impossible to describe.
Tulsidas describes the city: markets, gardens and huge armies of demon warriors guarding every side.
Seeing so many guards, Hanuman decides to take a tiny form and enter at night.
At the gate, Lankini, the city's guardian demoness, stops him.
Hanuman knocks her down with one blow. She remembers Brahma's prophecy: when a monkey strikes her, Lanka's end is near.
Lankini rejoices at seeing Ram's messenger and says a moment with the holy outweighs heaven itself.
She tells Hanuman to enter with Ram in his heart, for nothing is hard for one Ram favours.
Hanuman slips into the city and searches palace after palace, even Ravan's, but Sita is not there.
He finds a house marked with Ram's weapons and tulsi plants, and wonders how a good soul lives in Lanka.
Vibhishan wakes up chanting Ram's name. Hanuman, disguised as a Brahmin, calls out to him.
Vibhishan asks if the visitor is a devotee of Hari, or Ram himself.
Hanuman tells him Ram's story; both are overjoyed. Vibhishan says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth.
Vibhishan feels hopeful that Ram has sent this saint to him. Hanuman says Ram loves even a lowly monkey like him.
Vibhishan explains how Sita is kept and how Hanuman can reach her.
In the Ashok grove Hanuman finally sees Sita: thin, sorrowful, lost in thoughts of Ram. He hides in a tree.
Ravan arrives with his queens and tries to win Sita over with gifts, promises and threats.
Holding a blade of grass between them, Sita scorns him: can a firefly make the lotus bloom?
Furious at being called a firefly, Ravan draws his sword to kill her.
Sita answers that either Ram's arm or Ravan's sword will be around her neck, and nothing else.
Mandodari calms Ravan. He orders the demonesses to frighten Sita and gives her one month.
Trijata, a kind demoness, tells the others her dream of a monkey burning Lanka and Ravan's downfall.
The frightened demonesses fall at Sita's feet and leave. Sita fears the month will soon pass.
In despair, Sita begs Trijata to build a pyre so she can end her life. Trijata comforts her and leaves.
Alone, Sita begs the stars, the moon and the Ashok tree for fire to end her sorrow.
Seeing her pain, Hanuman drops Ram's ring. Sita catches it, thinking the tree has answered with an ember.
Sita recognises Ram's ring and is torn between joy and worry: how could it get here?
Hanuman, still hidden, begins softly telling Ram's story. Sita's sorrow lifts as she listens.
Sita asks the storyteller to show himself. Hanuman comes forward and says he is Ram's messenger.
Sita asks how a man and a monkey became friends; Hanuman tells her, and she trusts him.
Sita, moved to tears, calls Hanuman her boat in an ocean of grief and asks after Ram and Lakshman.
She asks whether Ram, so kind by nature, has forgotten her.
Hanuman gently assures her Ram loves her twice as much as she loves him.
Hanuman gives Ram's message: without Sita, everything around him feels like fire and pain.
Ram's message ends: his mind always stays with her. Sita is lost in love.
Hanuman asks Sita to take heart: Ram's arrows will burn the demons like moths in a flame.
Hanuman says Ram would have come already had he known where she was, and will come soon with his army.
Sita worries that the monkeys are small and the demons mighty. Hanuman shows his giant golden form.
Hanuman shrinks again: it is Ram's power, not his own, that makes the small defeat the mighty.
Sita blesses Hanuman: may he be ageless, immortal and full of virtue, and dear to Ram.
Hanuman says he is hungry. Sita warns him about the guards, then lets him eat the fruits.
Hanuman eats the fruit and starts uprooting trees. The guards run to tell Ravan.
Ravan sends soldiers; Hanuman crushes them. Then Ravan's son Akshay comes, and Hanuman kills him.
Furious at his son's death, Ravan sends his mightiest son Meghnad to capture Hanuman alive.
Hanuman and Meghnad fight like two great elephants. Meghnad cannot defeat him.
Meghnad fires the Brahmastra. To honour Brahma's weapon, Hanuman lets himself be bound.
Shiva remarks: Ram's name frees people from all bondage, yet his messenger lets himself be tied for Ram's work.
Demons gather to watch as Hanuman is brought to Ravan's splendid court. He stands there without fear.
Ravan laughs at him, then grieves for his son, and demands to know who he is.
Hanuman describes Ram: the power behind all creation, who broke Shiva's bow and killed Bali.
Hanuman says he only ate fruit when hungry and struck those who struck him.
Hanuman humbly urges Ravan to give up pride, return Sita, and seek Ram's forgiveness.
Hanuman warns that no one, not even Shiva, Vishnu or Brahma, can protect an enemy of Ram.
Ravan mocks his wise advice and orders the demons to kill him.
Vibhishan arrives and reminds Ravan that killing a messenger is wrong. Ravan agrees to another punishment.
Ravan orders the monkey's tail wrapped in oiled cloth and set on fire.
Hanuman smiles inwardly. He grows his tail until Lanka runs out of cloth and oil.
The demons parade Hanuman through the city, laughing and kicking, and set his tail alight.
Hanuman becomes tiny, slips free, and leaps onto the golden rooftops.
The winds blow at Hari's command. Hanuman grows huge and races from palace to palace, setting Lanka ablaze.
Lanka burns. The people cry out that this is surely a god, and the price of insulting a saint.
Only Vibhishan's house is spared. Hanuman, unharmed, jumps into the sea to put out his tail.
Hanuman returns to Sita and asks for a token to take to Ram. She gives him her crest-jewel.
Sita sends Ram a message: remember your vow to protect the helpless, and come within a month.
Sita says seeing Hanuman soothed her, but now her lonely days will return. He comforts her and leaves.
Hanuman roars as he leaves and leaps back across the sea. The monkeys rejoice as if born again.
The happy monkeys feast in Sugriv's Madhuban garden with Angad's permission, beating off the guards.
Sugriv guesses they must have found Sita. The monkeys arrive and tell him Hanuman saved them all.
Everyone goes to Ram, who is sitting on a crystal rock with Lakshman. All fall at his feet.
Jambavan praises Ram's grace and tells him of Hanuman's deeds. Ram embraces Hanuman.
Ram asks how Sita survives. Hanuman says Ram's name guards her life day and night.
Hanuman gives Ram Sita's crest-jewel and her message, asking what fault made Ram abandon her.
Hanuman says Sita's suffering is beyond words and begs Ram to go at once.
Ram weeps for Sita. Hanuman says Ram can easily defeat the demons and bring her back.
Ram tells Hanuman no one has ever helped him so much and he can never repay him.
Hanuman falls at Ram's feet, overwhelmed with love. Shiva, telling this story, is lost in the memory.
Ram asks how Hanuman burned Lanka. Hanuman humbly says it was all Ram's glory, not his own.
Hanuman asks only for unwavering devotion, and Ram grants it.
Ram tells Sugriv to prepare the army. The gods shower flowers.
Countless monkeys and bears gather. Ram's gracious glance fills them with strength.
Ram sets out amid good omens. Far away, Sita senses it, while Ravan sees bad omens.
The vast army marches, shaking the earth and the mountains, singing Ram's glory.
The army reaches the seashore and camps, eating fruit along the way.
In Lanka the demons live in fear since Hanuman burned the city.
Mandodari privately begs Ravan to return Sita before Ram's arrows destroy their clan.
Ravan laughs at her fears and boasts that the monkeys will just be food for his demons.
News comes that Ram's army has reached the shore. Ravan's ministers flatter him that there is nothing to fear.
Vibhishan comes to court and respectfully advises Ravan to give up another's wife and his pride.
Vibhishan explains that Ram is God himself in human form and protects all who seek refuge.
Vibhishan begs again at Ravan's feet. The wise minister Malyavan agrees with him.
Ravan calls them both fools. Vibhishan warns him that bad judgement has taken over his mind.
Ravan, furious, calls Vibhishan a traitor and kicks him. Vibhishan still holds his feet.
Vibhishan leaves Lanka with his ministers, announcing he will take refuge in Ram. Lanka's fortune leaves with him.
On his way, Vibhishan joyfully imagines seeing Ram's holy feet.
Vibhishan reaches the shore. The monkeys suspect a spy and tell Sugriv, who wants him bound.
Ram says his vow is to protect anyone who seeks refuge, whatever their past.
Ram explains that one who turns to him is freed of past sins, and only the pure-hearted reach him.
Ram tells them to bring Vibhishan either way. Hanuman, Angad and Sugriv bring him with respect.
Vibhishan sees Ram from afar and is spellbound by his beauty.
Vibhishan introduces himself as Ravan's brother and begs Ram for protection.
Ram rises with joy, embraces him and asks how he managed to live among the wicked.
Vibhishan says no one is truly well until Ram lives in their heart; now, seeing Ram, he is free of fear.
Ram describes the devotee he loves: one who ties all attachments into a rope that binds him to Ram's feet.
Vibhishan asks only for devotion. Ram anoints him king of Lanka with seawater; flowers rain from the sky.
Tulsidas says those who leave such a Lord for another are like beasts without tails or horns.
Ram asks how to cross the ocean. Vibhishan suggests first asking the ocean, an elder of Ram's clan.
Lakshman objects that only cowards rely on fate. Ram smiles and goes to sit on the shore to pray to the ocean.
Ravan's spies, disguised as monkeys, watch everything and are moved by Ram's kindness.
The monkeys catch the spies and start beating them. Lakshman frees them and gives them a letter for Ravan.
The spies return. Ravan mockingly asks about Vibhishan, the monkey army and the 'ascetics'.
Shuk tells Ravan that Vibhishan has been crowned, and describes the huge, fearsome monkey army.
Shuk names the great monkey heroes and says each is as strong as Sugriv, all eager for Ram's order.
Shuk says Ram could dry the ocean with one arrow, yet humbly asks it for a path. Ravan laughs.
Shuk hands over Lakshman's letter. Ravan has it read aloud: return Sita or perish.
Ravan laughs off the letter. Shuk begs him to make peace with Ram.
Ravan kicks Shuk, who goes to Ram and is freed from an old curse, becoming a sage again.
Three days pass and the ocean ignores Ram's prayer. Ram angrily asks Lakshman for his bow.
Ram aims a fiery arrow; the sea begins to boil. The ocean appears as a Brahmin bearing jewels.
The ocean begs forgiveness and promises to obey Ram.
The ocean reveals that Nal and Neel can make stones float, so a bridge can be built across the sea.
At the ocean's request, Ram uses his arrow on wicked people on its northern shore, then the ocean departs.
Sunderkand ends: Tulsidas says singing and hearing Ram's virtues carries one across the ocean of life.
Aarti to Hanuman: his strength, his help to saints, and his deeds for Ram.
Burning Lanka, bringing the Sanjivani, rescuing Ram and Lakshman from Ahiravan.
Gods, sages and Mother Anjana perform his aarti.
Aarti to the Ramayan itself, the story sung by gods, sages and saints.
